source: Sharma and Chopra (2025) The Sequential Edge: Inverse-Entropy Voting Beats Parallel Self-Consistency at Matched Compute
finding: Gap 1 and 3. At equal total tokens, k parallel chains with a vote lose to the same tokens spent as k sequential refinement steps in 43 of 45 settings. Inverse-entropy weighted voting beats plain majority in both modes.
numbers: 5 open models (20B to 235B), AIME-2024, AIME-2025, GPQA-Diamond. 3, 6, 9 chains, each up to 4096 tokens (6 chains = 24,576 tokens). Qwen3-235B AIME-2025 6 chains: sequential 76.7 vs parallel 30.0 (+46.7). Figure 1 GPQA-Diamond: gains 11 to 14.6 points. Wins 43/45 = 95.6%.
quote: sequential scaling where chains explicitly build upon previous attempts consistently outperforms the dominant parallel self-consistency paradigm in 95.6% of configurations
limits: Not a test of one long thinking pass: both arms use 4096-token chains. The small per-chain cap may truncate long-thinking models in the parallel arm; the paper reports no truncation rate (I found none). AIME has 30 items. Sequential needs serial calls (latency). Preprint, no replication found.
agent_relevance: Does not show vote loses to one long pass. Shows that at 4K-token chains, building on a previous attempt beats independent restarts. Test: compare vote-of-k against refine-k at equal tokens on our own tasks.

source: Mirzaei (2026) Sample More, Reflect Less: Self-Refine and Reflexion Lose to Repeated Sampling at Equal Token Cost, from 1.5B to 7B
finding: Gap 1 and 3. A designed, paired test at equal measured tokens: repeated sampling with a vote is never reliably beaten by any of 7 methods. All 18 comparisons with self-inspection (critique, refine, reflect, pick-best) come out negative.
numbers: Qwen2.5 1.5B, 3B, 7B; GSM8K and MATH-500, 150 questions each; 36 paired comparisons with 95% CIs and Holm correction. 10 methods reliably worse, 2 survive Holm. Best-of-N (model picks among 8) loses to plain count by 8.0 and 11.3 points at 1.5B, only 2.0 and 1.3 at 7B (not distinguishable from 0). Self-Refine and forced Reflexion stay 3.6 to 10.1 points below at 7B. SC on 1.5B GSM8K: 70.1 at N=1 (297 tokens) to 80.9 at N=16 (4749 tokens). Best-of-N 3B MATH-500 -14.1 [-20.0,-8.4].
quote: No method is reliably better than repeated sampling at equal cost in any setting.
limits: Small open models (1.5B to 7B), short CoT, math only; says nothing about frontier long-thinking models. 150 items per set. Single-author preprint. Unforced Reflexion never retried on the 1.5B model.
agent_relevance: Supports plain code-side vote over model self-selection at equal tokens, mainly for small models. At 7B an LLM picker is no longer clearly worse than counting, so recheck on the real model.

source: Iacobacci et al. (2025) Increasing the Thinking Budget is Not All You Need
finding: Gap 1. On Qwen3 thinking models, splitting a thinking budget over several calls with a vote or summary can beat spending it in one call, but the evidence is thin and noisy.
numbers: AIME24 only (30 problems; one item = 3.33 points). Thinking OFF, Qwen3-8B: vanilla 23.33, self-consistency 3x 33.33, SC 5x 30.00, Summary 3x 33.33, Summary 5x 30.00. Qwen3-4B: vanilla 23.33, SC 3x 20.00, SC 5x 33.33. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B: vanilla 10.00, SC 3x 10.00, SC 5x 6.67, Summary 5x 20.00. With thinking on, SC gave no improvement on the two weaker models (authors blame answer extraction).
quote: simply increasing the thinking budget is not the most effective use of compute
limits: One benchmark, 30 items, three small models, no confidence intervals; differences of 1 to 3 items. Authors list the narrow data as a limitation. Not usable as proof either way.
agent_relevance: Weak hint that a consolidating call over k answers (like USC) is competitive with a plain vote. Do not build on it without our own test.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Reasoning in Token Economies: Budget-Aware Evaluation of LLM Reasoning Strategies (EMNLP 2024)
finding: Gap 1 and 3. When compute is matched, chain-of-thought plus self-consistency matches or beats multi-agent debate, Reflexion, Tree of Thoughts, Plan-and-Solve and others. Debate gets worse with more rounds because agents converge.
numbers: Seven strategies, five datasets, five models including GPT-4 (abstract and contribution list). I read the abstract, contributions and discussion text; I did not extract per-cell table numbers. SC works best when the chance of a correct sample is above 50%.
quote: simple baseline like chain-of-thought self-consistency ... can be remarkably competitive
limits: Budgeted by tokens and queries on 2023-24 models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4). No reasoning models. Per-cell numbers not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Strong prior for using plain vote as the baseline every fancier S3/S8 operator must beat at equal tokens.

source: Ding (2026) When LLMs Agree, Are They Right? Auditing Self-Consistency and Cross-Model Agreement as Confidence Signals
finding: Gap 2 and 9. Vote share is a positive but weak, regime-dependent signal of correctness. It works for mid-tier models and for deciding how much to sample. It fails as a stand-alone trust score for the most consistent (frontier) model, which is over-confident.
numbers: 53 runners, K=50 samples at T=1.0, gpt-4.1 nano/mini/full, GPQA Diamond and AIME, 265,000 samples, 5,300 case rows, 394 cases. Spearman rho of vote share C with majority-correct M 0.20 to 0.59, all 12 cells positive after Holm. gpt-4.1: C=0.89 but rho(C,M)=0.20 on GPQA, no more accurate than mini; E2 contrast -0.18 [-0.31,-0.03]. C >= 0.8 on 77% of gpt-4.1 GPQA entries, and 48% of those are wrong. A vote-share-routed cascade was dominated by always using the mid-tier model. Part of GPQA agreement is positional (option-shuffle control).
limits: Data come from a student course cohort (runs not guaranteed independent); model snapshots not logged; only the OpenAI gpt-4.1 family plus an exploratory 3-model Claude check; GPQA has only 4 options so chance agreement is high. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Do not use a fixed vote-share threshold to release answers. Calibrate per model and task on our own data; shuffle option order before voting on multiple-choice; treat unanimous as a warning on frontier models.

source: Gu, Yu, Partovi Nia, Asgharian (2026) Pause and Reflect: Conformal Aggregation for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
finding: Gap 2 and 9. A threshold on the weighted vote share can be set from 200 labelled calibration items to control the rate of confident wrong answers. Abstaining helps only when the score separates right from wrong; where it does not (HotpotQA), nothing helps.
numbers: 4 small open models (R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, Qwen3-1.7B, Gemma-4-E4B, Qwen3-8B), m=16 paths, GSM8K, MATH, MATH-Hard, HotpotQA, 10 model-dataset configs, n_cal=200. Headline: 90.1% selective accuracy on GSM8K with under 5% abstention vs 82% for majority vote (R1-Distill-1.5B GSM8K plain-vote accuracy 0.822). Realized confident-error rate tracked the target within calibration/test noise. Largest gains at medium difficulty; HotpotQA frontier nearly flat.
limits: Small models, 16 samples, needs labelled calibration data per task and exchangeability. Weights come from a reward model, judge or perplexity, not plain counts. Preprint. Headline is one config, not an average.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete recipe for the stop/escalate rule: tune a vote-share threshold on about 200 labelled items, check score separability first, and escalate (verifier/search) instead of answering when below threshold.

source: Zollo, Wang, Zemel (2026) Binary Agreement for Efficient Unsupervised Confidence Calibration of Reasoning LLMs (BASC)
finding: Gap 2. Test-time self-consistency from 100 samples is a good unlabeled confidence signal: calibration error about as low as supervised recalibration and much better than token probabilities or verbalized confidence.
numbers: 36 model-dataset combinations (9 reasoning models, 5 tasks). ECE1 / Brier / AUROC: token probs 0.197 / 0.222 / 0.655; verbalized confidence 0.268 / 0.281 / 0.635; TT-SC (100 samples) 0.090 / 0.125 / 0.836; supervised recalibration 0.051 / 0.147 / 0.732; BASC-L (k=2) 0.083 / 0.162 / 0.685. TT-SC ECE by task: math 0.037, QA 0.144.
limits: Raw vote share ranks well (AUROC 0.836) but is less well calibrated on QA tasks (ECE 0.144). Needs 100 samples per query. BASC is a learned calibrator, outside scaffold-only scope. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Vote share ranks answers well; map it to a probability with a small isotonic/binned table per task rather than reading it as a probability. Verbalized confidence is much worse.

source: Komiyama, Oba, Oyamada (2026) Best-of-infinity: Asymptotic Performance of Test-Time LLM Ensembling
finding: Gap 3, 5, 7. In a best-of-5 test on AIME-2025 with GPT-OSS-20B, plain majority vote beat every other selector, including two LLM-as-judge variants, three reward models and self-certainty. Adaptive stopping on answer agreement cuts samples 2x to 5x.
numbers: Bo5 AIME-2025, GPT-OSS-20B, 16 trials, 2-sigma CI: Omniscient 91.04 +/- 1.32; majority 85.42 +/- 2.01; judge (tournament) 82.92 +/- 2.57; judge (set) 81.25 +/- 2.42; Skywork-Reward-V2-Qwen3-8B 80.00; INF-ORM-70B 79.79; Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-8B 79.79; self-certainty 75.83 +/- 2.47; random 76.25 +/- 2.71. Adaptive Bayes-factor stopping reached fixed-BoN accuracy with 2x to 5x less compute (MATH500, GPT-OSS-20B); about 80 samples usually enough. Weighted multi-LLM ensembles matched or beat the best single model in 106 of 165 three-model combinations (64.2%) when weights trained on AIME-2024 were tested on AIME-2025.
limits: Selector comparison is one model, one benchmark (30 items), N=5. Reward models were general ones, not trained for this model. Self-certainty sits at the random level here, in conflict with its own paper. Short-answer math only.
agent_relevance: At small N on short-answer tasks, code-side counting is a hard baseline to beat; judge and reward calls add cost and did not help. Also gives an adaptive stopping rule (stop when the leader is statistically ahead).

source: Nitarach (2026) Model Capability Dominates: Inference-Time Optimization Lessons from AIMO 3
finding: Gap 4. Giving different voters different reasoning prompts did not help; at temperature 1.0 the within-question votes were already not positively correlated, and weaker prompts cost more accuracy than they gained in independence.
numbers: AIMO 3 setting: 50 IMO-level problems, 3 models, 23+ experiments, one H100, 5 hours. gpt-oss-120b: baseline (T=1.0, 21-run mean) 39.3/50; T=0.5 38; T=0.8 40; T=1.2 37; best vote 42/50 vs pass@20 45.5 (selection loss). Equal prompt mix at T=0.5: 36 (worse than T=0.5 alone, 38). Estimated pairwise correlation of correct votes: all 19 computable points negative; mean -0.122 for N>=7; mean -0.348 over all 19 (N=3 points sit at the -0.5 floor).
quote: Every prompt-level intervention fails. High-temperature sampling already decorrelates errors
limits: Only 50 problems; a 1-point change is 2% and is noise. The correlation estimator conditions on each problem's own hit rate, so it cannot see the real failure: items where the model's chance of the right answer is under 50%. Competition math only, 3 models. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Do not spend tokens on persona or prompt-rewrite diversity at temperature about 1.0 for short-answer math. The remaining loss is selection loss (pick the right answer among those found), so spend on a selector or verifier, not more diversity.

source: Ali (2026) Where Cross-Question Structure in LLM Errors Comes From: Shared Seeds, Shared Prompts, and Answer-Letter Preference
finding: Gap 4 and 9. Independent draws from one model show no detectable structure of same-missing-knowledge across questions. Structure appears only if the passes share a random seed or a few-shot prompt, and in multiple choice a large part is a preference for an answer letter.
numbers: 24 models (including Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B); eigenvalue test of the question-by-question correlation matrix; K up to 100 passes, T=1. Llama-3.2-1B answers A in 81% of replies in original option order (fitted guess share 0.90 on A). Rotating the options moves the pattern with the letter. Counting a question correct only if right in all 4 rotations removes the guess-driven part.
limits: Tests structure across questions, not wrong-answer agreement within one question. Mostly small open models on multiple choice. Preprint. Does not measure how often the plurality answer is wrong.
agent_relevance: Two cheap fixes for the vote: give every sample its own seed (never share a seed or few-shot block across a pass) and randomise option order across samples on multiple-choice items.

source: Aghazadeh, Ghasemi, Beyhaghi, Pishro-Nik (2026) CGES: Confidence-Guided Early Stopping for Efficient and Accurate Self-Consistency
finding: Gap 5. With a budget of 16, early stopping saves the most on easy sets and the least on hard ones; a Bayesian rule that adds confidence scores saves more than earlier rules without losing accuracy, except where the confidence signal is uninformative.
numbers: Budget 16, 10 seeds, average calls per question (SC always 16.0). ESC (window 4): AIME24 10.68, GPQA 12.88, MATH500 7.74, GSM8K 5.16, MMLU-Pro 8.99; avg 9.09, accuracy -0.4 pp. CGES-LNS (arith): AIME24 7.77, GPQA 11.90, MATH500 5.99, GSM8K 2.41, MMLU-Pro 8.24; avg 7.26. Abstract: 58% fewer calls on average (16.0 to 6.7) within 0.4 pp. SC accuracy: AIME24 77.3, GPQA 50.0, MATH500 81.2, GSM8K 94.2, MMLU-Pro 62.1. On GPQA the posterior never concentrates and CGES neither saves calls nor fully matches SC.
limits: Budget only 16 samples; 7B-class models; AIME24 has 30 items. Works best when confidence scores carry signal. Author-reported; matching within 0.4 pp is an average, and GPQA lost about 2 pp.
agent_relevance: On hard items the saving is small (GPQA 12.9 of 16 calls, AIME24 10.7) because no answer leads early. Set budget by difficulty class and expect the hardest items to need nearly the full budget or escalation.

source: Fu, Wang, Tian, Zhao (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Gap 2, 3, 5. Filtering or weighting traces by internal confidence (token log-probs) lifts vote accuracy on hard reasoning sets and, used online, cuts generated tokens by up to 84.7%. It sometimes hurts when the model is confidently wrong.
numbers: Offline, 512 traces, 64 repeats. GPT-OSS-120B AIME25: pass@1 91.8, cons@512 97.0, DeepConf (tail, top 10%) 99.9. DeepSeek-8B: AIME24 83.0 / 86.7 / 93.3; HMMT25 58.1 / 69.6 / 79.5 (bottom-10%, top 10%) and 83.9 (tail); GPQA-D 62.8 / 72.5 / 74.0. Qwen3-32B GPQA-D 68.9 / 72.2 / 72.5. GPT-OSS-120B HMMT25 pass@1 78.9 / cons 92.9 / DeepConf top-10% 90.5 and 88.9 (worse than plain vote). Online: up to 84.7% fewer tokens.
limits: Needs token log-probs (not available for all closed APIs). Five benchmarks, mostly 30-item competition sets. Gains from 10% filtering vanish or reverse for an over-confident model. Authors flag confident-but-wrong traces as the key limitation.
agent_relevance: If logprobs are available, a confidence-filtered weighted vote is a drop-in upgrade, but keep plain vote as a fallback and test per model.

source: Shi and Jin (2025) Heimdall: test-time scaling on the generative verification
finding: Gap 7. A trained long-CoT verifier plus pessimistic selection beats plain majority vote at larger budgets. The selection rule falls back to majority vote when verification counts are small, so the two are one family.
numbers: Verification accuracy 62.5% to 94.5% after RL, 97.5% with repeated sampling (96.0% on AIME2025, 97.5% on AIME2024). DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B solver, AIME2025: pass@1 54.2%, 70.0% with 16x compute, 83.3% with more compute; majority vote converges to about 70%. With Gemini 2.5 Pro as solver: 93.0%. Majority vote was the worst of the scaling algorithms at equal N in their Figure 4.
quote: Majority Voting is trapped in the bias of the solver
limits: Verifier is specially trained (outside scaffold-only scope). 60 AIME questions. Verification is harder on AIME2025 than AIME2024.
agent_relevance: When vote plateaus because a wrong answer is the mode, a verifier on the top few distinct answers (not on every sample) is the cheaper hybrid. Their formula: grouped vote term plus verifier term, trusting the verifier more as counts grow.

source: Sareen et al. (2025) Putting the Value Back in RL: Better Test-Time Scaling by Unifying LLM Reasoners With Verifiers (RL^V)
finding: Gap 7. With a verifier trained together with the solver, weighted voting beats both plain majority vote and best-of-N once 8 or more solutions are sampled, on AIME 2024, for short- and long-CoT 1.5B models.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, AIME 2024 (30 items), 1 to 1024 solutions; weighted vote above majority vote at N>=8. Abstract: MATH accuracy up over 20% with parallel sampling, 8x to 32x more efficient test-time scaling than the base RL method, 1.2x to 1.6x higher when scaling parallel plus sequential with a long-reasoning model.
limits: Requires RL training of the verifier (outside scaffold-only). Small models, one hard 30-item set for the strategy comparison. A verifier prompt on the same untrained model is a weaker variant they also report.
agent_relevance: Voting still adds value after a verifier exists, as the weighting base. Use the verifier score as the weight, not as a replacement for counting.

source: Kang, Zhao, Song (2025) Scalable Best-of-N Selection for Large Language Models via Self-Certainty
finding: Gap 3 and 6. Ranking free-form samples by the model's own output-distribution sharpness (self-certainty) scales with N, needs no reward model, and beat universal self-consistency in the authors' tests.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, N up to 64, LiveBench-Math, GSM8K, MATH, CRUXEval-O. USC results were left out where over 20% of prompts exceeded the context window. Self-certainty and Borda-weighted voting led plain SC; the KL-based measure kept improving to N=64 while perplexity stopped helping at N>16. Per-cell values are garbled in my text extract, so none are recorded.
limits: Author-reported. In the independent Komiyama test (d08) self-certainty scored 75.83 vs random 76.25 on AIME-2025 with GPT-OSS-20B: no gain. Needs logprobs. Mostly short-answer sets, so the open-ended claim has little test.
agent_relevance: Cheap code-side selector if logprobs exist, but results disagree across models. Check on our model before trusting it.

source: OPPO AI Agent Team (2025) Scaling Test-time Compute for LLM Agents
finding: Gap 6. For tool-using agents on GAIA, selecting the final answer by majority vote across trajectories was worse than a list-wise judge that sees all candidates. Best-of-N sampling was the best way to use more compute; beam and tree search added little.
numbers: GAIA validation (165 tasks), GPT-4.1 agent, width 4. Baseline 55.76. Best-of-N about +8 points over baseline; BoN-wise about +3. Result merging in BoN: voting 56.8, scoring 59.39, list-wise 63.03. Beam search: voting 54.55, scoring 53.94, list-wise 56.97. Naive reflection 55.15 (below baseline); selective reflection (threshold <2) 56.36.
limits: One benchmark, one model, small N (4). The verifier is a process-reward-model prompt, not the same as our selector. How free-form agent answers were matched for voting is not described.
agent_relevance: On agent tasks with free-form answers a list-wise judge over all candidates beat counting by 6 points. Supports USC-style selection for S7 on open tasks, with vote used only when answers can be matched exactly.

source: Huang et al. (2025) m1: Unleash the Potential of Test-Time Scaling for Medical Reasoning with Large Language Models
finding: Gap 8. In medical QA, longer thinking helps only up to about 4K tokens, and extra budget forcing gave negligible benefit. This study did not test voting, so it answers gap 8 only by absence.
numbers: m1-7B-23K average 60.32% over in-distribution and out-of-distribution medical sets; gains from thinking budget saturate beyond about 4K tokens; difficulty-filtered data +0.27 to +0.65 points. No self-consistency curve reported.
limits: Not a vote study. Suggests the knowledge limit, not sample count, may bound accuracy in medicine. I found no clean held-out law, biology or causal-task voting study this session.
agent_relevance: A reason to expect vote gains to be limited when the failure is missing knowledge. Gap 8 stays open.

source: Fu et al. (2025) DeepConf GPQA rows with Aghazadeh et al. (2026) CGES GPQA and MMLU-Pro rows (non-math check)
finding: Gap 8. Voting still helps on a non-math science set (GPQA-Diamond), but by less than on competition math, and early stopping saves little there.
numbers: DeepConf GPQA-D, cons@512 vs pass@1: DeepSeek-8B 72.5 vs 62.8 (+9.7); Qwen3-32B 72.2 vs 68.9 (+3.3). CGES budget-16 SC on GPQA 50.0 and MMLU-Pro 62.1 (Qwen-7B class); ESC saves 3.1 of 16 calls on GPQA vs 10.8 on GSM8K. For comparison DeepSeek-8B pass@1 to cons@512: AIME24 +3.7, AIME25 +5.4, HMMT25 +11.5.
limits: GPQA has 198 items with 4 options; chance agreement is high and the ceiling is set by knowledge. Only GPQA and MMLU-Pro; no law, biology or causal tasks found. Numbers come from two papers and different models.
agent_relevance: Expect smaller, knowledge-limited gains on non-math items; budget fewer samples and escalate sooner.
